JFR Profiling

The runtime image includes jattach, not a full JDK. Replace <container> with the app container name.

# Start a bounded profile recording.
docker exec <container> jattach 1 jcmd \
  'JFR.start name=mtl_profile settings=profile maxage=30m maxsize=256m'

# Dump before stopping the container. An OOM SIGKILL cannot flush a recording.
docker exec <container> jattach 1 jcmd \
  'JFR.dump name=mtl_profile filename=/app/logs/mtl-profile.jfr'

# Inspect heap capacity and obtain a thread dump.
docker exec <container> jattach 1 jcmd 'GC.heap_info'
docker exec <container> jattach 1 jcmd 'Thread.print -l'

For container memory, use cgroup counters:

docker exec <container> cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current
docker exec <container> cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.peak
docker exec <container> cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events

The source image uses G1 with MaxRAMPercentage=40.0 and InitialRAMPercentage=6.25. At the default 1248 MiB app container limit, Java 25 G1 rounds the maximum heap to 500 MiB and the initial heap to 78 MiB. A 1176 MiB limit gives a 472 MiB maximum heap and a 74 MiB initial heap.

Demo preparation finishes before Java starts. The remaining 60% of the app limit covers JVM native allocations and the shared media process slot, which allows one libvips, ImageMagick, FFprobe or FFmpeg child at a time by default. Heap capacity is only part of the JVM's total memory usage. A synthetic 4K HEVC to 1080p HLS conversion used about 328 MiB of FFmpeg RSS; a 256 MiB helper container failed, while 384 MiB completed. Historical JVM native allocations were about 300 MiB. These separate measurements guide the budget; they do not establish a safe combined limit for every workload. A focused ARM64 check ran synthetic GPX imports and 1080p conversion together under the default app limit. Larger workloads and AMD64 memory peaks remain unverified. Larger media or more concurrent helpers may require a larger app limit.

Upgrade to an image containing this profile to apply the new percentage. Raising both Compose memory and swap limits and recreating the app container scales the heap according to the running image's percentage. Other limits or JVM options may change the effective heap; check it with GC.heap_info above.

Remove any fixed -Xmx override from JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, or a custom Java command when adopting automatic heap sizing. Keep unrelated JVM options. A fixed heap size takes precedence over the percentage. See container memory limits for the Compose settings.

The published 0.8.1 Dockerfile used ZGC with MaxRAMPercentage=50.0. ZGC process RSS could count multiple mappings of the same heap pages. Use cgroup usage and OOM events for container decisions, and inspect the running image's JVM arguments before comparing profiles.

On this page
  • Container memory limits

Container memory limits

The default Compose file uses these settings. Memory and swap limits are equal, which disables container swap.

Service Memory and swap limit Related settings
app 1248 MiB Image heap profile: 40%; routing timeout: MTL_PLANNER_BROUTER_TIMEOUT_MS=310000
db 512 MiB Keep the complete PostgreSQL command, including shared_buffers=64MB, work_mem=1MB, and max_connections=20
brouter 512 MiB BROUTER_JAVA_XMX=128m
location-search 128 MiB MTL_LOCATION_SEARCH_MMAP_SIZE=33554432 (32 MiB)
map-server (optional) 128 MiB LOWZOOM_MAXZOOM=6

The limits are at least 20 percent above historical validated limits: 640 MiB for the standard app, 384 MiB for PostgreSQL and BRouter, and 96 MiB for location search and maps. Those checks used earlier app workloads and heap settings; they do not establish a 20 percent margin for the current app with 1080p conversion. BRouter was checked with routes up to about 1,500 km. The map limit was checked while extracting its zoom 0-6 overview and serving concurrent range requests. Compose allows a routing request up to 310 seconds, just above BRouter's 300-second route ceiling. Large image or video conversions use the app headroom one at a time. Docker and the operating system need additional memory.

When raising a limit, set the memory and swap limits to the same value, then recreate the container. A process restart does not apply changed limits or environment settings.

Every installation uses a local Compose file, including copies held by NAS container managers. Compare it with the new release's template and merge the settings for every service you run. Keep your credentials, ports, mounts, and deliberately larger limits. Apply the related settings above together with their memory limits; copy the full PostgreSQL command from the template.

For the current image, the default app limit needs no fixed heap override. Merge this example into the existing app service:

services:
  app:
    memswap_limit: 1248m
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 1248m

Validate the edited Compose file with docker compose config --quiet, then recreate the affected services with docker compose up -d. With the current image, the default 1248 MiB limit, and no fixed heap override, the app startup log should report heapMaxMiB=500.0. Larger limits produce a larger heap; check the effective size with GC.heap_info.
